answers.title: Introduction
answers.question: What can you help me analyze? Give me a short tour of the portfolio and the kinds of questions you answer well.
answers.answer:
Here's the portfolio as of the data end date, 2026-07-13.

**Portfolio snapshot**
- **80 advertisers** across **10 industries**, with 8 advertisers in each industry (Healthcare, Financial Services, Real Estate, Travel, Restaurants, Auto, Retail, Insurance, Education, B2B SaaS).
- **144 engine accounts** (Google Ads and Microsoft Advertising), **1,024 campaigns**.
- **15 agencies** across four tiers. **58 advertisers** have an active agency engagement; the other 22 are self-managed.
- **$20.48M** of spend in the 30 days to 2026-07-13 (engine aggregate).

**Questions I answer well**
- **Efficiency:** CPA, ROAS, CTR, CPC and conversion rate, with a breakdown of why CPA moved (CPC or conversion rate).
- **Engines and devices:** Google vs Microsoft, and Mobile vs Desktop vs Tablet.
- **Budget and bidding:** which campaigns are pacing hard against budget, and which Target CPA campaigns miss their target.
- **Impression share:** budget-limited Search campaigns, and top-of-page share by engine.
- **Keyword and search term waste:** zero-conversion keywords, low quality score keywords, broad-match overflow, and wasteful search terms.
- **Attribution:** how channels open and close paths, path length, time to conversion, and channel value under six models. The data-driven model is a non-production simulation, so I treat it as illustrative only.
- **Agencies:** which agency and tier manage the top advertisers, and how the book spreads across tiers.
- **Trends:** daily spend, conversions and CPA.

Each conversion answer names its source. Engine aggregate figures cover campaign, engine and device efficiency. Floodlight events cover channels and attribution. The search term aggregate covers keyword waste. I don't add these sources together.

Good starting questions: "Which Target CPA campaigns miss their target, and by how much?" or "How do Display and Paid Search compare under first-click and last-click?"

answers.title: Account Structure
answers.question: Count the advertisers, engine accounts, campaigns, ad groups and keywords in the portfolio, and trace how each level contains the next. Put the count on each level. Show it as a flowchart.
answers.answer:
The portfolio has 80 advertisers, 144 engine accounts, 1,024 campaigns, 4,621 ad groups and 33,399 keywords. Every level sits fully under the one above it: no advertiser lacks an engine account, no account lacks a campaign, and no campaign lacks an ad group.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Advertisers: 80"] -->|"1.8 engine accounts each"| B["Engine accounts: 144"]
    B -->|"7.1 campaigns each"| C["Campaigns: 1,024"]
    C -->|"4.5 ad groups each"| D["Ad groups: 4,621"]
    D -->|"7.2 keywords each"| E["Keywords: 33,399"]
```

Each ratio is the count below divided by the count above, so it is an average across the portfolio. Those ratios are plain counts, not performance metrics.

One gap: 460 ad groups (about 10%) have no keyword. They are still counted in the ad-group total, and their campaigns are fully covered by the hierarchy.

The counts come from the base tables with no date window, so they describe the whole portfolio, including any paused or inactive items. Engine accounts are counted directly, not through agency or status filters.

answers.title: Budget Pacing
answers.question: Over the last 7 days, list the ten campaigns with the highest pacing. Give me the campaign name, spend, the budget in effect, and pacing. Show it as a Markdown table, and show the SQL you ran.
answers.answer:
Over the 7 days ending 2026-07-13, the ten campaigns spending furthest ahead of their budgets were all Search campaigns running 7% to 13% over. Pacing is total spend divided by the sum of the daily budgets in effect for each day.

| Campaign | Spend (7d) | Budget in effect (7d) | Pacing |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|
| Silver Path Co Search 01 | $8,139.82 | $7,218.75 | 112.76% |
| Harbor Labs Co Search 04 | $17,004.68 | $15,383.06 | 110.54% |
| Crescent Gate Co Search 03 | $3,741.36 | $3,391.99 | 110.30% |
| Cedar Haven Co Search 05 | $12,699.97 | $11,540.76 | 110.04% |
| Harbor Line Co Search 03 | $20,366.35 | $18,709.56 | 108.86% |
| Harbor Stone Co Search 01 | $17,012.19 | $15,730.75 | 108.15% |
| Lake Labs Co Search 05 | $5,552.05 | $5,152.00 | 107.76% |
| Union Grove Co Search 02 | $7,017.01 | $6,518.33 | 107.65% |
| Pioneer Field Co Search 05 | $12,464.42 | $11,595.78 | 107.49% |
| Crescent Labs Co Search 04 | $5,061.94 | $4,709.25 | 107.49% |

Harbor Line Co Search 03 has the largest overspend in dollars, at about $1,657 above its budget. Silver Path Co Search 01 has the highest pacing ratio, but it is one of the smaller campaigns.

The spend comes from the engine aggregate (`daily_stats.cost`). The window covers report dates 2026-07-07 through 2026-07-13.

The first query failed because Snowflake rejected a correlated subquery. I rewrote the budget lookup as a join that keeps the latest budget version on or before each day. The query below is the one that produced the table.

```sql
WITH campaign_day AS (
    SELECT ds.campaign_id, ds.report_date, SUM(ds.cost) AS cost
    FROM daily_stats ds
    CROSS JOIN v_reference_date r
    WHERE ds.report_date > DATEADD(day, -7, r.reference_date)
      AND ds.report_date <= r.reference_date
    GROUP BY ds.campaign_id, ds.report_date
), budget_in_effect AS (
    SELECT cd.campaign_id, cd.report_date, cb.daily_budget
    FROM campaign_day cd
    JOIN campaign_budget cb
      ON cb.campaign_id = cd.campaign_id
     AND cb.effective_date <= cd.report_date
    QUALIFY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY cd.campaign_id, cd.report_date
                               ORDER BY cb.effective_date DESC) = 1
), with_budget AS (
    SELECT cd.campaign_id, cd.cost, be.daily_budget
    FROM campaign_day cd
    LEFT JOIN budget_in_effect be
      ON be.campaign_id = cd.campaign_id
     AND be.report_date = cd.report_date
)
SELECT c.campaign_name,
       ROUND(SUM(wb.cost), 2) AS spend_7d,
       ROUND(SUM(wb.daily_budget), 2) AS budget_in_effect_7d,
       ROUND(SUM(wb.cost) / NULLIF(SUM(wb.daily_budget), 0), 4) AS pacing_pct
FROM with_budget wb
JOIN campaign c ON c.campaign_id = wb.campaign_id
GROUP BY c.campaign_id, c.campaign_name
ORDER BY pacing_pct DESC
LIMIT 10
```

One caveat: a campaign-day with no budget version yet in effect adds spend but no budget, which would inflate its pacing. I did not check whether any of these ten campaigns has that case.

answers.title: Engine Choice
answers.question: Over the last 30 days, compare Google Ads and Microsoft Advertising on cost per click, conversion rate and CPA. Explain why the CPAs end up where they do, and say whether that is a reason to shift budget.
answers.answer:
**Short answer:** Microsoft Advertising has a lower CPA, but the gap is small (about 5%). It is not enough on its own to justify moving budget from Google.

**Engine comparison, last 30 days (to 2026-07-13, engine aggregate conversions)**

| Metric | Google Ads | Microsoft Advertising |
| :--- | ---: | ---: |
| Spend | $13.03M | $7.45M |
| Clicks | 5.94M | 4.06M |
| CPC | $2.19 | $1.83 |
| CTR | 3.74% | 3.74% |
| Conversion rate | 4.32% | 3.81% |
| CPA | $50.85 | $48.16 |

**Why the CPAs land where they do**

CPA is CPC divided by conversion rate. Microsoft's clicks cost 16% less, but they convert about 12% less often. The two effects nearly cancel, so the CPA gap is only about $2.70.

CTR is identical on both engines, so the difference is not in who clicks. It is in what each click costs and whether it converts.

The mix is not the cause. Search makes up about 87–88% of spend on both engines. Comparing only the 64 advertisers that run on both engines gives the same picture: Google $51.21 CPA, Microsoft $48.16.

**Where the pattern reverses**
- **Search:** Microsoft is cheaper ($48.02 vs $51.44 CPA).
- **Display:** Microsoft is cheaper ($45.73 vs $51.60).
- **Shopping:** Microsoft is more expensive ($53.48 vs $45.55). Its CPC is similar, but its conversion rate is lower (3.68% vs 4.25%).

**Should budget shift?**

Not on this evidence alone. Three reasons:
1. The blended gap is about 5%, and average CPA is not the same as the CPA of the next dollar.
2. Microsoft has about 32% fewer impressions than Google. Adding spend there could push its CPC up, which would erase the advantage.
3. Each engine reports its own conversions, so the two CPAs are not a perfectly common yardstick.

A reasonable next step is a controlled Search test that moves a modest amount of budget to Microsoft and tracks marginal CPA. Shopping should not move toward Microsoft based on this data.

Source: engine aggregate (`daily_stats.conversions`). I did not use Floodlight conversions here, since this is an engine efficiency question. A debug report has been written.

answers.answer:
**102 of the 118 Target CPA campaigns with spend in the last 30 days ran above their target CPA.** The table shows the 20 furthest over target, ranked by how far over they are. Window: 2026-06-13 to 2026-07-13. Conversions come from the engine aggregate (`daily_stats`).

| Campaign | Target CPA (USD) | Actual CPA (USD) | Over target |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| Silver Path Co Search 07 | 2.82 | 27.89 | +889% |
| Silver Path Co Search 01 | 2.82 | 22.34 | +692% |
| North Crest Co Search 05 | 3.64 | 27.48 | +651% |
| Silver Path Co Display 02 | 2.82 | 19.86 | +604% |
| Silver Path Co Search 06 | 2.82 | 19.26 | +583% |
| Bright Line Co Search 04 | 4.17 | 27.84 | +568% |
| Silver Path Co Display 04 | 2.82 | 18.53 | +557% |
| Silver Works Co Shopping 05 | 21.88 | 140.55 | +542% |
| North Crest Co Search 06 | 3.64 | 22.96 | +531% |
| Bright Line Co Display 03 | 4.17 | 26.21 | +529% |
| Silver Path Co Search 06 | 2.82 | 17.58 | +523% |
| Lake Haven Co Search 03 | 3.85 | 23.50 | +510% |
| Lake Haven Co Shopping 02 | 3.85 | 22.61 | +487% |
| Silver Works Co Search 03 | 21.88 | 128.41 | +487% |
| Silver Works Co Search 02 | 21.88 | 128.08 | +485% |
| Summit Stone Co Search 03 | 26.05 | 140.46 | +439% |
| Silver Works Co Shopping 02 | 21.88 | 117.75 | +438% |
| Lake Haven Co Shopping 01 | 3.85 | 20.64 | +436% |
| Summit Stone Co Search 06 | 26.05 | 136.43 | +424% |
| Silver Works Co Search 06 | 21.88 | 114.56 | +424% |

Notes:
- Two campaigns are both named "Silver Path Co Search 06". They are different campaign rows, so the name alone does not identify one.
- The gaps are very large. Some campaigns are at 5 to 9 times their target. Several Silver Path, North Crest, Bright Line and Lake Haven campaigns have targets under $5, while the Silver Works and Summit Stone targets are above $20. I have not checked whether those targets are set correctly.

SQL run:

```sql
WITH camp AS (
    SELECT c.campaign_id,
           c.campaign_name,
           bs.target_cpa,
           SUM(ds.cost) AS cost,
           SUM(ds.conversions) AS conversions
    FROM campaign c
    JOIN bid_strategy bs ON bs.bid_strategy_id = c.bid_strategy_id
    JOIN bid_strategy_type bst ON bst.bid_strategy_type_id = bs.bid_strategy_type_id
    JOIN daily_stats ds ON ds.campaign_id = c.campaign_id
    CROSS JOIN v_reference_date r
    WHERE bst.type_name = 'Target CPA'
      AND bs.target_cpa IS NOT NULL
      AND ds.report_date > DATEADD(day, -30, r.reference_date)
      AND ds.report_date <= r.reference_date
    GROUP BY c.campaign_id, c.campaign_name, bs.target_cpa
)
SELECT campaign_name,
       ROUND(target_cpa, 2) AS target_cpa,
       ROUND(cost / NULLIF(conversions, 0), 2) AS actual_cpa,
       ROUND((cost / NULLIF(conversions, 0)) / target_cpa - 1, 4) AS over_target_pct
FROM camp
WHERE cost / NULLIF(conversions, 0) > target_cpa
ORDER BY over_target_pct DESC
LIMIT 20
```

answers.title: Where Search Spend Goes
answers.question: Over the last 30 days, split search term spend into spend matched to a keyword and broad-match overflow, then split each into spend with and without conversions. Put the dollar amount on each step. Show it as a flowchart.
answers.answer:
Over the 30 days ending 2026-07-13, search term spend totaled **$1,168,922.28**. Almost all of it sits on terms that converted, and zero-conversion waste is small. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Total search term spend
$1,168,922.28"] --> B["Matched to a keyword
$1,025,494.02"] A --> C["Broad-match overflow
$143,428.26"] B --> D["With conversions
$1,018,589.52"] B --> E["No conversions
$6,904.50"] C --> F["With conversions
$135,045.74"] C --> G["No conversions
$8,382.52"] ``` - **Keyword-matched:** 87.7% of total spend. Only $6,904.50 (0.7% of this branch) sits on terms with no conversions. - **Broad-match overflow:** 12.3% of total spend. $8,382.52 (5.8% of this branch) sits on terms with no conversions, a higher share than keyword-matched spend. - **Zero-conversion waste:** $15,287 in total, about 1.3% of spend. Conversions come from the search term aggregate (`search_term_report.conversions`). A term counts as converting if its summed conversions over the window are above zero. The split reconciles: the two branches add to the total, and each pair of conversion states adds to its branch.

answers.title: Top Advertisers
answers.question: List the ten advertisers with the most spend over the last 30 days. Give me the advertiser name, the managing agency, spend, and ROAS. Show it as a Markdown table, and show the SQL you ran.
answers.answer:
The ten advertisers with the most spend over the 30 days ending 2026-07-13 are below. Cedar Path Co leads at about $450K. Two of the ten are self-managed. ROAS ranges from 2.32 (Blue Haven Co) to 11.46 (Harbor Stone Co).

| Advertiser | Managing agency | Spend (30d) | ROAS |
|:--|:--|--:|--:|
| Cedar Path Co | Silver Point Media | $449,763.09 | 3.27 |
| Blue Haven Co | Summit Ridge Media | $447,789.99 | 2.32 |
| Lake Forge Co | Cedar Field Media | $426,579.64 | 6.71 |
| Iron Peak Co | (self-managed) | $403,956.90 | 8.45 |
| Summit Stone Co | (self-managed) | $399,314.90 | 2.75 |
| Crescent Gate Co | North Field Media | $395,062.16 | 2.74 |
| Iron Ridge Co | Bright Peak Media | $371,785.75 | 3.40 |
| Crescent Point Co | Summit Field Media | $352,848.33 | 6.49 |
| Harbor Path Co | Summit Field Media | $348,254.70 | 3.72 |
| Harbor Stone Co | Summit Gate Media | $337,196.06 | 11.46 |

ROAS is conversion value divided by spend, using the engine aggregate (`daily_stats.conversion_value`). Each of the ten has at most one active agency engagement, so no spend is double-counted.

```sql
WITH adv_spend AS (
    SELECT ea.advertiser_id,
           SUM(ds.cost) AS spend_30d,
           SUM(ds.conversion_value) AS conv_value_30d
    FROM daily_stats ds
    CROSS JOIN v_reference_date r
    JOIN campaign c ON c.campaign_id = ds.campaign_id
    JOIN engine_account ea ON ea.engine_account_id = c.engine_account_id
    WHERE ds.report_date > DATEADD(day, -30, r.reference_date)
      AND ds.report_date <= r.reference_date
    GROUP BY ea.advertiser_id
),
active_agency AS (
    SELECT ac.advertiser_id, COUNT(*) AS n_active, MIN(ac.agency_id) AS agency_id
    FROM agency_client ac
    WHERE ac.is_active = 1
    GROUP BY ac.advertiser_id
)
SELECT a.advertiser_name,
       COALESCE(ag.agency_name, '(self-managed)') AS agency_name,
       ROUND(s.spend_30d, 2) AS spend_30d,
       ROUND(s.conv_value_30d / NULLIF(s.spend_30d, 0), 2) AS roas,
       aa.n_active
FROM adv_spend s
JOIN advertiser a ON a.advertiser_id = s.advertiser_id
LEFT JOIN active_agency aa ON aa.advertiser_id = s.advertiser_id
LEFT JOIN agency ag ON ag.agency_id = aa.agency_id
ORDER BY s.spend_30d DESC
LIMIT 10
```

answers.title: Customer Journey
answers.question: Trace how conversion paths move through the funnel: how many conversions start with an upper, mid and lower funnel channel, and how many end with each. Put the count on each stage. Show it as a flowchart.
answers.answer:
Most conversion paths open upstream and close downstream. Upper-funnel channels start 56% of paths but finish only 8%, while lower-funnel channels finish 73%. This covers 5,000 Floodlight conversions over the 90-day Floodlight window ending 2026-07-13.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    U1[Starts upper: 2,816] -->|2,041 end lower| L2[Ends lower: 3,629]
    U1 -->|554 end mid| M2[Ends mid: 974]
    U1 -->|221 end upper| U2[Ends upper: 397]
    M1[Starts mid: 928] -->|663 end lower| L2
    M1 -->|191 end mid| M2
    M1 -->|74 end upper| U2
    L1[Starts lower: 1,256] -->|925 end lower| L2
    L1 -->|229 end mid| M2
    L1 -->|102 end upper| U2
```

| Stage | Starts path (first touch) | Share | Ends path (last touch) | Share |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Upper | 2,816 | 56.3% | 397 | 7.9% |
| Mid | 928 | 18.6% | 974 | 19.5% |
| Lower | 1,256 | 25.1% | 3,629 | 72.6% |

- The largest flow is upper to lower: 2,041 conversions, about 41% of all conversions.
- Only 221 paths both start and end upper. Upper channels mostly open paths and hand them to lower channels.
- Under last-click, the lower funnel gets most of the credit. Attribution models that credit earlier touches would show a bigger upper-funnel contribution. For channel-level credit under all six models, see `mv_attribution_six_models`. Its data-driven column is a non-production simulation, illustrative only.

answers.title: Path Length
answers.question: How many touches do conversion paths take, and what share of conversions have more than two touches? Say whether paths are long enough for the choice of attribution model to matter.
answers.answer:
**Short answer:** Most conversion paths are longer than one touch, and 60% have three or more touches. That is long enough for the attribution model to matter, and the models disagree sharply.

**Path length (Floodlight events, all 5,000 conversions in `attribution_path`)**

| Touches | Conversions | Share |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 2 | 1,997 | 39.9% |
| 3 | 1,476 | 29.5% |
| 4 | 739 | 14.8% |
| 5 | 551 | 11.0% |
| 6 | 237 | 4.7% |

- The typical path has 2 or 3 touches. The mean is not computed here, but the distribution is skewed toward short paths with a long tail.
- **Conversions with more than two touches: 3,003 of 5,000, or 60.1%.**
- Paths start at a minimum of 2 touches, so no conversion is a single-touch path.

**Does the model choice matter?**

Yes. The same $2.11M of conversion value is split very differently by each model. The totals match across models, so the difference is only in who gets the credit:

| Model | Display | Paid Search |
|---|---:|---:|
| First-click | $643.7K | $450.4K |
| Last-click | $62.2K | $1,351.8K |
| Linear | $360.3K | $810.5K |
| Position-based | $356.8K | $858.8K |
| Time-decay | $310.0K | $886.0K |

Display earns $644K under first-click but only $62K under last-click. Last-click gives Paid Search about three times the credit it gets under first-click, which is the lower-funnel bias described in the attribution notes. With 60% of paths running three or more touches, the middle models (linear, position-based, time-decay) are where the upper-funnel channels get a fair share.

Notes:
- Source: Floodlight events (`conversion` and `attribution_path`). The query covers all paths in the table, which spans the 90-day Floodlight window ending 2026-07-13. I did not filter by date.
- The `data_driven_simulated` model is a non-production simulation, illustrative only. Its Display and Paid Search values are $384K and $795K. I did not use it for the conclusions above.
